title: Adapting a big model to your needs
hook: Prompting, examples, light fine-tuning, full fine-tuning, distillation, preference tuning.
inPlainWords: Changing a big model's behavior is a ladder, from cheapest to costliest. Stop at the first rung that passes your tests.

useCase.title: Make replies sound like ShopEase and follow the policy format
useCase.story: Replies must use ShopEase's friendly voice, always end with a next step, and follow a fixed layout. You have 300 approved past replies.

approaches.name: Instructions in the prompt
approaches.what: Describe the voice and layout in words.
approaches.avoidWhen: The rules are too subtle to describe.
approaches.example: "Friendly, brief, end with a next step."

approaches.name: Examples in the prompt
approaches.what: Show three to five approved replies.
approaches.greatWhen: A quick way to transfer style.
approaches.avoidWhen: Prompts get long and costly with too many rules.

approaches.name: Light fine-tuning
approaches.what: Train a small add-on layer instead of the whole model.
approaches.greatWhen: A consistent style or format, with hundreds to thousands of examples.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need new facts. Use RAG instead.
approaches.example: Train an add-on with the 300 approved replies.

approaches.name: Full fine-tuning
approaches.what: Update all of the model's weights.
approaches.greatWhen: You have lots of data, a big budget, and a need for deep specialization.
approaches.avoidWhen: Small data. It risks forgetting other skills, and costs a lot.
approaches.example: A lab training a specialist medical model.

approaches.name: Distillation
approaches.what: Train a small model to copy a big model's answers.
approaches.greatWhen: A steady, high-volume, narrow task where cost and delay matter.
approaches.example: A small model writes replies at a fraction of the cost.

approaches.name: Preference tuning
approaches.what: Teach the model which of two answers people prefer.
approaches.example: Agents pick the better of two draft replies.

challenge.question: You have 300 approved replies. What is the smart order of attack?

options.text: Instructions and examples first, then light fine-tuning only if your test set still fails
options.why: You climb only as far as you need to, and you measure at each step.

options.text: Fine-tune the policy facts into the model
options.why: Facts change. Keep them in retrieval.

options.text: Skip prompting and go straight to light fine-tuning
options.why: It can work, but you may never have needed it.

bestCase.title: Climb the cheapest rung that passes your test
bestCase.example: Instructions and three examples get 85% of replies approved. Light fine-tuning on 300 replies lifts it to 95%. Policy facts stay in RAG, so a policy change needs no retraining.

worstCase.title: Fine-tuning first, on messy examples, for facts
worstCase.example: A full fine-tune on 200 replies of mixed quality. The model copies a careless agent's typos, forgets how to follow other instructions, and still quotes last year's policy.

route.travelling: Draft reply to a late-parcel complaint

steps.label: Write instructions
steps.goes: Voice, layout and the next-step rule, in words.

steps.label: Add a few examples
steps.goes: Three approved replies show the voice.

steps.label: Light fine-tune if needed
steps.goes: Train an add-on with 300 approved replies. Now 95% are approved.
steps.goesWrong: A full fine-tune runs on 200 messy replies, with no test set.

steps.label: Keep facts in RAG
steps.goes: Policy text is retrieved, not baked in.

takeaway: Change behavior with the cheapest tool that passes your tests. Facts stay in retrieval, not in the weights.
